analysis.one_liner: Designates the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, permanently barring oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the Arctic Refuge coastal plain wilderness never got a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have put about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the coastal plain known as the 1002 Area — into the National Wilderness Preservation System. Wilderness designation is the strongest land protection in U.S. law: no roads, no development, and no oil drilling, permanently. The bill was read once in the Senate and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the permanent protection would have belonged to everyone who values unspoiled public land: visitors to the refuge, wildlife such as caribou and migratory birds that use the coastal plain, and future generations who would inherit the area undeveloped rather than opened to oil exploration. It would also have settled, permanently, a fight that has recurred for decades over whether to drill there.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public land users and future generations

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge — the coastal plain shown on a 1991 Interior Department map as the '1002 Area, Alternative E' — as wilderness under the Wilderness Act [S3].
It amends the National Wildlife Refuge System Administration Act of 1966 to add this land to the National Wilderness Preservation System, the strictest protection federal land can carry [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on oil companies and the state of Alaska's drilling revenue prospects: the coastal plain is believed to sit above significant oil reserves, and wilderness status would have closed it to exploration permanently. Anyone arguing for domestic drilling access would bear the opportunity cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies seeking Arctic drilling access

drawbacks.text: The coastal plain is the one part of the Arctic Refuge with real oil potential; wilderness designation would permanently lock away that resource, and drilling supporters argued it could reduce domestic oil supply [S3].
Alaska's economy has historically relied on oil revenue and oil jobs, and the state's congressional delegation has long opposed wilderness designation of the coastal plain for that reason.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is between a permanent national environmental asset and a one-time-to-long-term stream of oil revenue. Wilderness designation is irreversible — once designated, the land cannot be opened to drilling by a future Congress without new legislation — which is exactly why supporters wanted it and why drilling advocates opposed it. The bill was straightforward in design: a single designation with a defined acreage and an existing government map.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator William Roth introduced the bill on April 9, 1997, joined by 17 other senators in the original introduction; all but Roth were Democrats [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced — the last action recorded for it [S5].
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 105th Congress ended [S5].
The bill was introduced again by others in later Congresses; the fight over the Arctic Refuge coastal plain has recurred repeatedly without resolution.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the coastal plain remained outside wilderness protection, keeping open the possibility of a future Congress voting to allow drilling there — the outcome oil companies and drilling advocates wanted. The public got no new protection and the decades-long dispute simply carried over.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drilling advocates and the oil industry

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, but all 19 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican senator beyond Roth supported the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have permanently closed the Arctic Refuge coastal plain — the largest unexplored, potentially productive onshore oil area in the U.S. — to drilling, so the industry's interest ran directly against the bill. Its death kept the option of a future drilling vote alive.
Wilderness status would preserve the undisturbed landscape that attracts visitors to the refuge, but with essentially no development there today, the immediate economic effect is small either way.
